title: Berry Compote
subtitle: Mixed berries cooked briefly with sugar, a quick, glossy sauce for yoghurt and porridge
excerpt: Berry compote is ten minutes on the hob and a jar in the fridge that makes every breakfast better for a week. Blueberries, strawberries, and blackberries cooked briefly with a little sugar until they slump and release their juice into a loose, glossy sauce. It keeps well and freezes even better, the kind of thing worth making in a double batch.
sourceNotes: Fruit compote is a French technique, the word comes from the Latin composita, meaning a mixture, widely adopted across British home cooking. A compote differs from jam in cooking time: jam is reduced until it sets firmly; compote is cooked briefly until the fruit softens and releases its juices without fully breaking down.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Thaw overnight in the fridge or gently in a pan over low heat.
recipe.batchNotes: Keeps in the fridge in a sealed jar for up to 1 week. Double the batch and freeze half in portions.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Keeps for a week in the fridge. Better after a day when the flavours have had time to settle.

glossaryTerms.definition: Fresh or dried fruit cooked briefly with sugar and a little liquid until the fruit softens and releases its juices into a loose, glossy sauce. Unlike jam, it is not reduced to the point of setting, it stays spoonable.

content.text: A
compote

is the most useful thing you can make with a surplus of summer berries, and the simplest. {{blueberries}} Blueberries, {{strawberries}} strawberries, and {{blackberries}} blackberries go into a pan with {{caster-sugar}} caster sugar and a small squeeze of {{lemon-juice}} lemon juice. The lemon isn't for flavour so much as for structure; it brightens the fruit and keeps the colour vivid. Ten minutes of gentle heat and the berries slump and release their juice into a loose, glossy sauce. It will sit in the fridge and improve every breakfast you spoon it over for the next week. The difference from jam is time and reduction: a
compote
stays pourable and the fruit holds some shape; jam is reduced until it sets hard enough to spread on toast.
How to make it

Hull and halve the {{strawberries}} strawberries. Put all the berries, {{blueberries}} blueberries, {{strawberries}} strawberries, and {{blackberries}} blackberries, into a small saucepan. Add the {{caster-sugar}} caster sugar, {{lemon-juice}} lemon juice, and {{vanilla-extract}} vanilla extract if using. Stir to combine.

Place over a medium-low heat. As the pan heats, the sugar dissolves into the juice released by the berries. Stir gently every minute or so. Within 3 to 4 minutes the mixture will be bubbling steadily and the berries will start to soften and break down at the edges. Continue cooking for another 5 to 6 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is glossy and has thickened slightly. Some berries should still hold their shape while others have fully broken down, that uneven texture is part of what makes a
compote
interesting.
Remove from the heat and leave to cool for a few minutes. It thickens further as it cools. Transfer to a clean jar with a lid. Use warm or cold.
What to do with it
Spoon over porridge in the morning, the contrast between the sweet-sharp compote and plain oats is excellent.
Use it to fill the yoghurt parfait from this collection in place of fresh fruit for an out-of-season winter version.
Stir through overnight oats before refrigerating. The compote soaks in overnight and colours the whole batch purple.
Serve warm alongside pancakes, French toast, or waffles.
Swirl through plain yoghurt for a quick, colourful breakfast with no other preparation needed.
Troubleshooter
Compote too thin: cook for another 2 to 3 minutes to reduce further. Bear in mind it thickens considerably as it cools.
Compote too thick after cooling: add a tablespoon of water or orange juice and stir over low heat to loosen.
Too sweet: add a small extra squeeze of lemon juice to balance. The acidity brightens the flavour and cuts through excessive sweetness.
Fruit all broken down: the heat was too high or it cooked too long. Use medium-low heat and watch it closely. A compote should finish in 8 to 10 minutes total.
